claim: The mammalian ORMDL proteins (ORMDL1, 2 and 3) mediate feedback inhibition of the de novo synthesis pathway of sphingolipids by inhibiting serine palmitoyl transferase in response to elevated ceramide levels.
source: The mammalian ORMDL proteins (ORMDL1, 2 and 3) mediate feedback inhibition of the de novo synthesis pathway of sphingolipids by inhibiting serine palmitoyl transferase in response to elevated ceramide levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work establishing this mechanism, as well as the experimental data in the manuscript showing elevated sphingolipids when ORMDLs are deleted.

claim: Ormdl1 and Ormdl3 function redundantly to suppress the levels of bioactive sphingolipid metabolites during myelination of the sciatic nerve.
source: We found that Ormdl1 and Ormdl3 function redundantly to suppress the levels of bioactive sphingolipid metabolites during myelination of the sciatic nerve.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data showing that Ormdl1/3 double KO mice have elevated sphingolipid levels in sciatic nerve and myelination defects, while single KOs do not show severe phenotypes.

claim: Without proper ORMDL-mediated regulation of sphingolipid synthesis, severe dysmyelination results.
source: Without proper ORMDL-mediated regulation of sphingolipid synthesis, severe dysmyelination results.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data showing abnormal myelin morphology in Ormdl1/3 double KO mice.

claim: The Ormdls function to restrain sphingolipid metabolism in order to limit levels of dangerous metabolic intermediates that can interfere with essential physiological processes such as myelination.
source: Our data indicate that the Ormdls function to restrain sphingolipid metabolism in order to limit levels of dangerous metabolic intermediates that can interfere with essential physiological processes such as myelination.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing elevated toxic sphingolipid intermediates in Ormdl1/3 double KO mice and the resulting myelination defects.

claim: The sphingolipid metabolic pathway is a fundamental feature of all eukaryotic cells.
source: The sphingolipid metabolic pathway is a fundamental feature of all eukaryotic cells (Merrill, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established scientific literature.

claim: The sphingolipid metabolic pathway is required to produce complex sphingolipids, such as sphingomyelin and the expansive glycosphingolipid family, that are plasma-membrane building blocks.
source: It is required to produce complex sphingolipids, such as sphingomyelin and the expansive glycosphingolipid family, that are plasma-membrane building blocks.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about sphingolipid function.

claim: The sphingolipid metabolic pathway generates bioactive metabolites (such as ceramide, sphingosine, and sphingosine-1-phosphate) that alter cell activities, including growth regulation and apoptosis, through interactions with receptors and enzymes.
source: It also generates bioactive metabolites (such as ceramide, sphingosine, and sphingosine-1-phosphate) that alter cell activities, including growth regulation and apoptosis, through interactions with receptors and enzymes.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about bioactive sphingolipid metabolites.

claim: The de novo sphingolipid biosynthetic pathway begins with the condensation of an amino acid (usually serine) and a fatty acyl-CoA (usually palmitoyl-CoA) by the serine palmitoyltransferase (SPT) enzyme complex.
source: The de novo sphingolipid biosynthetic pathway begins with the condensation of an amino acid (usually serine) and a fatty acyl-CoA (usually palmitoyl-CoA) by the serine palmitoyltransferase (SPT) enzyme complex (Figure 1A) (Merrill, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The first product of the de novo sphingolipid biosynthetic pathway, 3-keto-dihydrosphingosine, is reduced to form dihydrosphingosine.
source: The first product, 3-keto-dihydrosphingosine, is then reduced to form dihydrosphingosine, which is subsequently acylated with fatty acids of different chain lengths to produce dihydroceramide.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge of the sphingolipid biosynthetic pathway.

claim: Dihydrosphingosine is acylated with fatty acids of different chain lengths to produce dihydroceramide.
source: The first product, 3-keto-dihydrosphingosine, is then reduced to form dihydrosphingosine, which is subsequently acylated with fatty acids of different chain lengths to produce dihydroceramide.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge of the sphingolipid biosynthetic pathway.

claim: Introduction of a double bond into the sphingoid base generates ceramide, a central metabolic intermediate in the pathway.
source: Introduction of a double bond into the sphingoid base generates ceramide, a central metabolic intermediate in the pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge of the sphingolipid biosynthetic pathway.

claim: Ceramide and its degradation product sphingosine are bioactive and can cause cell death at elevated levels.
source: Ceramide, and its degradation product sphingosine, are bioactive and can cause cell death at elevated levels (Hannun and Obeid, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Complex sphingolipids – sphingomyelin and glycosphingolipids – are generated by addition of hydrophilic head groups to the ceramide anchor.
source: Complex sphingolipids – sphingomyelin and glycosphingolipids – are generated by addition of hydrophilic head groups to the ceramide anchor.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge of sphingolipid biosynthesis.

claim: Three mammalian Ormdl genes exist (Ormdl1, Ormdl2, and Ormdl3).
source: Three mammalian Ormdl genes exist (Ormdl1, Ormdl2, and Ormdl3), and they encode small transmembrane endoplasmic reticulum proteins with amino-acid identities of around 80% (Hjelmqvist et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The three mammalian Ormdl genes encode small transmembrane endoplasmic reticulum proteins with amino-acid identities of around 80%.
source: Three mammalian Ormdl genes exist (Ormdl1, Ormdl2, and Ormdl3), and they encode small transmembrane endoplasmic reticulum proteins with amino-acid identities of around 80% (Hjelmqvist et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The ORMDL proteins, in complex with SPT, have the capacity to sense elevated ceramide levels and to inhibit SPT enzymatic activity.
source: The ORMDL proteins, in complex with SPT, have the capacity to sense elevated ceramide levels and to inhibit SPT enzymatic activity, thereby blocking entry of de novo synthesized sphingolipid substrate into the sphingolipid biosynthetic pathway (Davis et al., 2019; Han et al., 2019; Siow et al., 2015) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Ormdl1 KO mice were produced by CRISPR/Cas9-induced mutations, resulting in frameshifts and premature stop codons.
source: Ormdl1 and Ormdl2 KO mice were produced by CRISPR/Cas9-induced mutations, resulting in frameshifts and premature stop codons.
evidence: This claim is supported by the description in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Ormdl2 KO mice were produced by CRISPR/Cas9-induced mutations, resulting in frameshifts and premature stop codons.
source: Ormdl1 and Ormdl2 KO mice were produced by CRISPR/Cas9-induced mutations, resulting in frameshifts and premature stop codons.
evidence: This claim is supported by the description in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Ormdl3 KO mice were generated by germline Cre-LoxP recombination to excise exons 2, 3, and part of exon 4, resulting in the deletion of the entire protein-coding sequence.
source: Ormdl3 KO mice were generated by germline Cre-LoxP recombination to excise exons 2, 3, and part of exon 4, resulting in the deletion of the entire protein-coding sequence.
evidence: This claim is supported by the description in the text and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: RT-qPCR mRNA expression assays using brain RNA indicated a deficiency of the individual wild-type Ormdl mRNA expression in the corresponding KO mouse.
source: RT-qPCR mRNA expression assays using brain RNA with probes corresponding to the deleted coding sequences indicated a deficiency of the individual wild-type (WT) Ormdl mRNA expression in the corresponding KO mouse, consistent with the introduced genomic changes (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Ormdl1 KO mice had levels of dihydrosphingosine, dihydroceramide, ceramide, and sphingosine that were generally similar to those measured in WT mice.
source: The Ormdl1 KO and Ormdl2 KO mice had levels of these four types of sphingolipids that were generally similar to those measured in WT mice
evidence: This claim is supported by sphingolipid measurements shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Ormdl2 KO mice had levels of dihydrosphingosine, dihydroceramide, ceramide, and sphingosine that were generally similar to those measured in WT mice.
source: The Ormdl1 KO and Ormdl2 KO mice had levels of these four types of sphingolipids that were generally similar to those measured in WT mice
evidence: This claim is supported by sphingolipid measurements shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Ormdl3 KO mice had significantly elevated brain levels of dihydrosphingosine, dihydroceramide, ceramide, and sphingosine compared with WT mice.
source: however, the Ormdl3 KO mice had significantly elevated brain levels of each of these sphingolipids compared with WT mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by sphingolipid measurements shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Amongst the Ormdls, Ormdl3 has the greatest influence on the levels of sphingolipids generated solely through de novo synthesis.
source: This result suggests that amongst the Ormdls, Ormdl3 has the greatest influence on the levels of these sphingolipids, including those generated solely through de novo synthesis, consistent with ORMDL inhibitory action on SPT (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing that Ormdl3 KO mice have elevated sphingolipid levels while Ormdl1 and Ormdl2 KO mice do not.

claim: Ormdl1 KO, Ormdl2 KO, and Ormdl3 KO mice appeared overtly normal, with body weights not significantly different from those of WT mice at 8 weeks of age.
source: Ormdl1 KO, Ormdl2 KO, and Ormdl3 KO mice appeared overtly normal, with body weights not significantly different from those of WT mice at 8 weeks of age (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Intercross mating between respective single Ormdl KO mice produced litter sizes at weaning similar to those obtained through WT matings.
source: Intercross mating between respective single Ormdl KO mice produced litter sizes at weaning similar to those obtained through WT matings, suggesting normal fecundity and perinatal survival of Ormdl1 KO, Ormdl2 KO, and Ormdl3 KO mice (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by litter size data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Total amounts of dihydrosphingosine, dihydroceramide, ceramide, and sphingosine were not increased above WT levels in Ormdl1/2 double KO brain.
source: Total amounts of these four sphingolipid groups were not increased above WT levels in Ormdl1/2 double KO brain (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by sphingolipid measurements shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Levels of dihydrosphingosine, dihydroceramide, ceramide and sphingosine in Ormdl1/3 double KO brain substantially exceeded those of the Ormdl3 single KO mice.
source: However, levels of dihydrosphingosine, dihydroceramide, ceramide and sphingosine in Ormdl1/3 double KO brain substantially exceeded those of the Ormdl3 single KO mice (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by sphingolipid measurements shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Ormdl2/3 double KO brain dihydrosphingosine and dihydroceramide levels were significantly elevated above WT levels, but not to the extent observed in Ormdl1/3 double KO mouse brain.
source: Ormdl2/3 double KO brain dihydrosphingosine and dihydroceramide levels were significantly elevated above WT levels, but not to the extent observed in Ormdl1/3 double KO mouse brain (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by sphingolipid measurements shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: At 8 weeks of age, Ormdl1/2 and Ormdl2/3 double KO males and females had body weights similar to those of WT mice.
source: At 8 weeks of age, Ormdl1/2 and Ormdl2/3 double KO males and females had body weights similar to those of WT mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Both male and female Ormdl1/3 double KO mice weighed significantly less than WT mice at 8 weeks of age.
source: However, both male and female Ormdl1/3 double KO mice weighed significantly less than WT mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Ormdl1/2 double KO and Ormdl2/3 double KO mice were fertile and produced litter sizes similar to those of WT mating pairs when intercrossed.
source: Ormdl1/2 double KO and Ormdl2/3 double KO mice were fertile and, when intercrossed, produced litter sizes similar to those of WT mating pairs (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by litter size data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The Ormdl1/3 double KO mice exhibited abnormal hindlimb clasping upon tail suspension, a sign of possible neurodegeneration.
source: The Ormdl1/3 double KO mice exhibited abnormal hindlimb clasping upon tail suspension, a sign of possible neurodegeneration (Figure 2C) (Lalonde and Strazielle, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by observation shown in Figure 2C and citation to literature on this behavioral sign.

claim: The performance of Ormdl1, Ormdl2, and Ormdl3 single KO mice and of Ormdl1/2 and Ormdl2/3 double KO mice in the wire hang test was not significantly different from that observed for the WT mice.
source: The performance of Ormdl1, Ormdl2, and Ormdl3 single KO mice and of Ormdl1/2 and Ormdl2/3 double KO mice was not significantly different from that observed for the WT mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by wire hang test data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The latency time to fall from the wire was significantly shorter for Ormdl1/3 double KO mice than for WT mice in the wire hang test.
source: However, the latency time to fall from the wire was significantly shorter for Ormdl1/3 double KO mice than for WT mice, indicating that Ormdl1/3 double KO mice had a behavioral deficit related to limb strength and coordination.
evidence: This claim is supported by wire hang test data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Ormdl1/3 double KO mice had a behavioral deficit related to limb strength and coordination.
source: However, the latency time to fall from the wire was significantly shorter for Ormdl1/3 double KO mice than for WT mice, indicating that Ormdl1/3 double KO mice had a behavioral deficit related to limb strength and coordination.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the wire hang test results.

claim: No triple Ormdl1/2/3 KO mice were identified at weaning, although eight were predicted from the total number of offspring produced.
source: Notably, no triple Ormdl1/2/3 KO mice were identified, although eight were predicted from the total number of offspring produced.
evidence: This claim is supported by genotyping data shown in Table 1.

claim: The absence of all six WT Ormdl alleles causes either embryonic or neonatal lethality prior to weaning.
source: The results suggest that the absence of all six WT Ormdl alleles causes either embryonic or neonatal lethality prior to weaning.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the absence of triple KO mice at weaning.

claim: Inheritance of only one WT Ormdl2 or Ormdl3 allele substantially reduced viability.
source: Supporting this conclusion is the observation that inheritance of only one WT Ormdl2 or Ormdl3 allele substantially reduced viability.
evidence: This claim is supported by the reduced numbers of mice with only one WT Ormdl allele shown in Table 1.

claim: Ormdl1/3 double KO mouse sciatic nerve exhibited a highly abnormal morphology when compared with sciatic nerve obtained from WT or single Ormdl1 and Ormdl3 KO mice.
source: Ormdl1/3 double KO mouse sciatic nerve exhibited a highly abnormal morphology when compared with sciatic nerve obtained from WT or single Ormdl1 and Ormdl3 KO mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy images shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The nerves from the Ormdl1/3 double KO mice had a significantly lower frequency of myelinated axons per field compared with WT sciatic nerves.
source: The nerves from the Ormdl1/3 double KO mice had a significantly lower frequency of myelinated axons per field compared with WT sciatic nerves (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by axon density quantification shown in Figure 3B.

claim: No significant difference in the numbers of myelinated axons was observed between sciatic nerves from WT and Ormdl1 or Ormd3 single KO mice.
source: No significant difference in the numbers of myelinated axons was observed between sciatic nerves from WT and Ormdl1 or Ormd3 single KO mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by axon density quantification shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A significantly higher frequency of redundant myelin was observed in sciatic nerves from Ormdl1/3 double KO mice compared with WT mice.
source: A significantly higher frequency of redundant myelin, generally appearing as myelin 'outfoldings' (Golan et al., 2013), was also observed in sciatic nerves from Ormdl1/3 double KO mice compared with WT mice (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of redundant myelin shown in Figure 3D and example images in Figure 3C.

claim: Sciatic nerve of Ormdl1 KO mice had levels of dihydrosphingosine, dihydroceramide, ceramide, and sphingosine that were not significantly different from those from WT mice.
source: Sciatic nerve of Ormdl1 KO mice had levels of these sphingolipids that were not significantly different from those from WT mice
evidence: This claim is supported by sphingolipid measurements in sciatic nerve shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Sciatic nerve of Ormdl3 KO mice had significantly elevated levels of both dihydroceramide and ceramide compared with nerve from WT mice.
source: whereas sciatic nerve of Ormdl3 KO mice had significantly elevated levels of both dihydroceramide and ceramide compared with nerve from WT mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by sphingolipid measurements in sciatic nerve shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The Ormdl1/3 double KO sciatic nerve had significantly elevated levels of dihydrosphingosine, dihydroceramide, ceramide, and sphingosine compared with levels observed in the Ormdl3 KO mice.
source: However, the Ormdl1/3 double KO sciatic nerve had significantly elevated levels of all four of these sphingolipid species compared with levels observed in the Ormdl3 KO mice (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by sphingolipid measurements in sciatic nerve shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Hexosylceramide levels in the Ormdl1 and Ormdl3 single KO sciatic nerve were significantly increased compared to those in WT sciatic nerve.
source: Hexosylceramide levels in the Ormdl1 and Ormdl3 single KO sciatic nerve were significantly increased compared to those in WT sciatic nerve (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by hexosylceramide measurements shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Sciatic nerve from Ormdl1/3 double KO mice had decreased hexosylceramide levels, even though they had an 8-fold increase in the level of ceramide.
source: However, sciatic nerve from Ormdl1/3 double KO mice had decreased hexosylceramide levels, even though they had an 8-fold increase in the level of ceramide, the direct precursor for hexosylceramide synthesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by sphingolipid measurements shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The large increase in precursor sphingolipid substrate ceramide may have saturated the terminal glycosylation step for hexosylceramide production in Ormdl1/3 double KO mice.
source: This result suggests that the large increase in precursor sphingolipid substrate ceramide may have saturated the terminal glycosylation step for hexosylceramide production.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that hexosylceramide levels decreased despite elevated ceramide levels.

claim: Elevated sphingolipid synthesis resulting from Ormdl1/3 deficiency causes dysmyelination and motor-function abnormalities in mice.
source: Our results are consistent with the conclusion that elevated sphingolipid synthesis resulting from Ormdl1/3 deficiency causes dysmyelination and motor-function abnormalities in mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined data showing elevated sphingolipids, dysmyelination, and behavioral deficits in Ormdl1/3 double KO mice.

claim: Reductions in the synthesis of specific sphingolipids have been associated with defects in myelination.
source: Although reductions in the synthesis of specific sphingolipids have been associated with defects in myelination (Coetzee et al., 1996), it has not been shown previously that increased de novo sphingolipid synthesis can cause myelination defects.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: It has not been shown previously that increased de novo sphingolipid synthesis can cause myelination defects.
source: Although reductions in the synthesis of specific sphingolipids have been associated with defects in myelination (Coetzee et al., 1996), it has not been shown previously that increased de novo sphingolipid synthesis can cause myelination defects.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of the existing literature.

claim: After administration of pIpC, the fSPT polypeptide was detected by Western blotting in Stop-fSPT/Mx1-Cre mouse liver.
source: After administration of pIpC, the fSPT polypeptide was detected by Western blotting, along with significantly increased SPT enzymatic activity, in Stop-fSPT/Mx1-Cre mouse liver compared with the liver of mouse controls carrying only Stop-fSPT (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: SPT enzymatic activity was significantly increased in Stop-fSPT/Mx1-Cre mouse liver after pIpC administration compared with the liver of mouse controls carrying only Stop-fSPT.
source: After administration of pIpC, the fSPT polypeptide was detected by Western blotting, along with significantly increased SPT enzymatic activity, in Stop-fSPT/Mx1-Cre mouse liver compared with the liver of mouse controls carrying only Stop-fSPT (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by SPT activity assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Ceramide levels were significantly increased in the liver of mice expressing fSPT compared with that of control mice.
source: Ceramide levels were significantly increased in the liver of mice expressing fSPT compared with that of control mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ceramide measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Stop-fSPT/iPlp1-Cre mice that had been fed the tamoxifen diet exhibited severe hindlimb paralysis after 2 weeks.
source: After 2 weeks, the Stop-fSPT/iPlp1-Cre mice that had been fed the tamoxifen diet exhibited severe hindlimb paralysis (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the observation shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Sciatic nerve expression of the fSPT protein was confirmed by Western blotting in Stop-fSPT/iPlp1-Cre mice.
source: Sciatic nerve expression of the fSPT protein was confirmed by Western blotting (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Transmission EM analysis of sciatic nerves from fSPT-overexpressing mice revealed reduced axon density.
source: Transmission EM analysis of sciatic nerves from fSPT-overexpressing mice revealed reduced axon density (Figure 4C and D) and a significantly increased frequency of redundant myelin structures (Figure 4E and F), similar to those found in Ormdl1/3 double KO mice (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Transmission EM analysis of sciatic nerves from fSPT-overexpressing mice revealed a significantly increased frequency of redundant myelin structures, similar to those found in Ormdl1/3 double KO mice.
source: Transmission EM analysis of sciatic nerves from fSPT-overexpressing mice revealed reduced axon density (Figure 4C and D) and a significantly increased frequency of redundant myelin structures (Figure 4E and F), similar to those found in Ormdl1/3 double KO mice (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: Levels of dihydrosphingosine, total dihydroceramide, total ceramide, and sphingosine were significantly elevated in the sciatic nerves of the fSPT-expressing mice compared with those of control mice.
source: Levels of dihydrosphingosine, total dihydroceramide, total ceramide, and sphingosine were significantly elevated in the sciatic nerves of the fSPT-expressing mice compared with those of control mice (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by sphingolipid measurements shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Hexosylceramide levels were decreased in sciatic nerves of fSPT-expressing mice even though these mice had highly elevated ceramide levels.
source: However, as in the Ormdl1/3 double KO mice, hexosylceramide levels were decreased in sciatic nerves of fSPT-expressing mice even though these mice had highly elevated ceramide levels (Figure 4G – Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by sphingolipid measurements shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The ORMDLs have been identified as regulators that mediate feedback inhibition of de novo sphingolipid synthesis to control sphingolipid levels.
source: The ORMDLs have been identified as regulators that mediate feedback inhibition of de novo sphingolipid synthesis to control sphingolipid levels (Breslow et al., 2010; Davis et al., 2019; Hagen-Euteneuer et al., 2012; Zhakupova et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: ORMDLs are believed to act by sensing elevations in ceramide levels and by inhibiting SPT through direct protein–protein interactions within a multi-subunit enzyme complex.
source: They are believed to act by sensing elevations in ceramide levels and by inhibiting SPT through direct protein–protein interactions within a multi-subunit enzyme complex (Davis et al., 2019), although elevated free and phosphorylated sphingoid bases have also been suggested to inhibit SPT via ORMDLs (Hagen-Euteneuer et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Elevated free and phosphorylated sphingoid bases have also been suggested to inhibit SPT via ORMDLs.
source: They are believed to act by sensing elevations in ceramide levels and by inhibiting SPT through direct protein–protein interactions within a multi-subunit enzyme complex (Davis et al., 2019), although elevated free and phosphorylated sphingoid bases have also been suggested to inhibit SPT via ORMDLs (Hagen-Euteneuer et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: ORMDLs are functionally important modulators of in vivo sphingolipid levels in the nervous system.
source: The results presented here establish ORMDLs as functionally important modulators of in vivo sphingolipid levels in the nervous system.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing elevated sphingolipid levels in the nervous system of Ormdl KO mice.

claim: Mice lacking both Ormdl1 and Ormdl3 exhibit abnormal myelination in the sciatic nerve.
source: By evaluating mice in which either one or combinations of two of the three Ormdl genes were deleted, we found that mice lacking both Ormdl1 and Ormdl3 exhibit abnormal myelination in the sciatic nerve, as well as highly elevated sphingolipid levels in the nervous system.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data showing myelination defects in Ormdl1/3 double KO mice.

claim: Mice lacking both Ormdl1 and Ormdl3 exhibit highly elevated sphingolipid levels in the nervous system.
source: By evaluating mice in which either one or combinations of two of the three Ormdl genes were deleted, we found that mice lacking both Ormdl1 and Ormdl3 exhibit abnormal myelination in the sciatic nerve, as well as highly elevated sphingolipid levels in the nervous system.
evidence: This claim is supported by sphingolipid measurements in brain and sciatic nerve of Ormdl1/3 double KO mice.

claim: When de novo synthesis of sphingolipids was directly increased in myelin-producing cells by overexpression of fSPT, phenotypic manifestations similar to those seen in the Ormdl1/3 double KO mice occurred.
source: When de novo synthesis of sphingolipids was directly increased in myelin-producing cells by overexpression of fSPT, phenotypic manifestations similar to those seen in the Ormdl1/3 double KO mice occurred.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing that fSPT overexpression causes similar myelination defects and sphingolipid elevations as seen in Ormdl1/3 double KO mice.

claim: ORMDLs suppress sphingolipid levels that, when elevated, cause dysmyelination.
source: These findings indicate that ORMDLs suppress sphingolipid levels that, when elevated, cause dysmyelination.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined data from Ormdl KO mice and fSPT overexpression experiments.

claim: After birth, during the acute phase of myelination, the Schwann cell membrane surface area expands several thousand times.
source: After birth, during the acute phase of myelination, the Schwann cell membrane surface area expands several thousand times (Webster, 1971).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The myelin membrane is approximately 70–80% lipid by weight, with much of the non-sterol lipid made up of sphingolipids.
source: The myelin membrane is approximately 70–80% lipid by weight, with much of the non-sterol lipid made up of sphingolipids (Wattenberg, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The formation of the myelin membrane requires an extremely high influx of new substrate through the sphingolipid biosynthetic pathway to produce the mature sphingolipids needed for proper myelin formation.
source: Thus, the formation of the myelin membrane requires an extremely high influx of new substrate through the sphingolipid biosynthetic pathway to produce the mature sphingolipids, largely galactosylceramide and sulfated galactosylceramide, that are needed for proper myelin formation (Coetzee et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the high lipid content of myelin and supported by citation.

claim: Under conditions of very high sphingolipid synthesis, a lack of feedback inhibition could lead to high levels of ceramide if ceramide production exceeded the capacity of the downstream pathway to convert it into mature sphingolipids.
source: Under conditions of very high sphingolipid synthesis, a lack of feedback inhibition could lead to high levels of ceramide if ceramide production exceeded the capacity of the downstream pathway to convert it into mature sphingolipids.
evidence: This claim is a logical inference based on pathway kinetics.

claim: The Ormdl1/3 double KO mouse sciatic nerve contained high levels of ceramide together with lower levels of the mature sphingolipid hexosylceramide.
source: Indeed, we found that the Ormdl1/3 double KO mouse sciatic nerve contained high levels of ceramide together with lower levels of the mature sphingolipid hexosylceramide.
evidence: This claim is supported by sphingolipid measurements in Ormdl1/3 double KO sciatic nerve.

claim: The lower density of myelinated axons in the sciatic nerve of Ormdl1/3 double KO mice may be a consequence of cell death due to build-up of toxic sphingolipid precursor metabolites.
source: The lower density of myelinated axons in the sciatic nerve of Ormdl1/3 double KO mice may be a consequence of cell death due to this build-up of toxic sphingolipid precursor metabolites (Hannun and Obeid, 2018; Riley and Merrill, 2019).
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the data and supported by citations about ceramide toxicity.

claim: A key physiological function of the ORMDLs is to keep de novo sphingolipid synthesis in check so that ceramide production does not exceed the metabolic capacity of the cell to convert ceramide into mature, non-toxic sphingolipids.
source: Our findings are consistent with the idea that a key physiological function of the ORMDLs is to keep de novo sphingolipid synthesis in check so that ceramide production does not exceed the metabolic capacity of the cell to convert ceramide into mature, non-toxic sphingolipids that are destined for physiological processes (Davis et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental findings and supported by citation.

claim: Redundant myelination is believed to occur because of excessive myelin membrane growth or improper lipid composition.
source: Redundant myelination, often observed as loops of myelin growing into the Schwann cell cytoplasm or surrounding the axon outside the normal myelin sheath, is believed to occur because of excessive myelin membrane growth or improper lipid composition (Golan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Unbalanced sphingolipid synthesis, caused either by deletion of the Ormdls in the Ormdl1/3 double KO mice or by the overexpression of fSPT in myelin-producing cells, may have promoted the formation of myelin with abnormal lipid composition through the excessive production of sphingolipid precursors relative to mature sphingolipids.
source: Unbalanced sphingolipid synthesis, caused either by deletion of the Ormdls in the Ormdl1/3 double KO mice or by the overexpression of fSPT in myelin-producing cells, may have promoted the formation of myelin with abnormal lipid composition through the excessive production of sphingolipid precursors relative to mature sphingolipids.
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the observed redundant myelination and sphingolipid imbalances.

claim: Incorrect sphingolipid composition, caused by a deficiency of galactosyceramide, has been shown to produce redundant myelin profiles.
source: Incorrect sphingolipid composition, caused by a deficiency of galactosyceramide, has been shown to produce redundant myelin profiles (Dupree et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease often features redundant myelination as its prominent histologic feature.
source: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, an inherited demyelinating neuropathy, often features redundant myelination as its prominent histologic feature (Cotter et al., 2010; Goebbels et al., 2012; Golan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A distinct Charcot-Marie-Tooth phenotype in humans is caused by deficiency in the sphingolipid degradation enzyme, S1P lyase, a condition that can elevate ceramide levels.
source: Interestingly, a distinct Charcot-Marie-Tooth phenotype in humans is caused by deficiency in the sphingolipid degradation enzyme, S1P lyase, a condition that can elevate ceramide levels (Atkinson et al., 2017; Prasad et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The ORMDLs may be needed for embryonic or neonatal viability.
source: These data suggest that the ORMDLs may also be needed for embryonic or neonatal viability.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the absence of triple KO mice and reduced numbers of mice with only one WT Ormdl allele.

claim: During embryonic growth, high levels of de novo sphingolipid synthesis would be required to support the extensive cellular proliferation that occurs.
source: During embryonic growth, high levels of de novo sphingolipid synthesis would be required to support the extensive cellular proliferation that occurs (Hojjati et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Immediately after birth, de novo sphingolipid synthesis is elevated in epidermal cells to supply specialized sphingolipids in support of skin barrier formation.
source: Immediately after birth, de novo sphingolipid synthesis is also elevated in epidermal cells to supply specialized sphingolipids in support of skin barrier formation (Holleran et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The lack of negative feedback control on sphingolipid biosynthesis caused by the absence of ORMDLs in the Ormdl triple KO mice may have disrupted critical developmental processes in which sphingolipids play an essential role.
source: The lack of negative feedback control on sphingolipid biosynthesis caused by the absence of ORMDLs in the Ormdl triple KO mice may have disrupted these or other critical developmental processes in which sphingolipids play an essential role.
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the lethality of triple KO mice.

claim: The individual ORMDLs can partially compensate for each other in both the control of sphingolipid levels and to prevent expression of severe phenotypes.
source: Our results indicate that the individual ORMDLs can partially compensate for each other in both the control of sphingolipid levels and to prevent expression of severe phenotypes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that single KO mice have mild or no phenotypes while double KO mice have severe phenotypes.

claim: Redundancy of ORMDL function may reflect an organismal advantage in having robust control over a pathway that generates toxic metabolites but is also required under certain developmental scenarios to produce extremely high levels of specialized sphingolipid end-products.
source: The reason for redundancy of ORMDLs may reflect an organismal advantage in having robust control over a pathway that generates toxic metabolites but is also required under certain developmental scenarios to produce extremely high levels of specialized sphingolipid end-products.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about the evolutionary advantage of ORMDL redundancy.

claim: Under circumstances of high metabolic flux, small perturbations in downstream enzyme activities or transport mechanisms could result in catastrophic consequences if ceramide levels were allowed to increase.
source: Under circumstances of high metabolic flux, small perturbations in downstream enzyme activities or transport mechanisms could result in catastrophic consequences if ceramide levels were allowed to increase.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about the importance of ORMDL regulation.

claim: The existence of multiple ORMDL isoforms may reflect independent functions for the ORMDLs, such as differential responses to individual ceramide species according to their chain length, degree of saturation, or some other aspect of structure.
source: The existence of multiple isoforms may also reflect independent functions for the ORMDLs, such as differential responses to individual ceramide species according to their chain length, degree of saturation, or some other aspect of structure.
evidence: This claim is speculative about potential functional differences between ORMDL isoforms.

claim: In Ormdl1/3 double KO brain, dihydroceramides with very long chain fatty acids (C22-26) did not increase, whereas in Ormdl1/3 double KO sciatic nerve, dihydroceramides with very long chain fatty acids were highly elevated.
source: Interestingly, in Ormdl1/3 double KO brain, dihydroceramides with very long chain fatty acids (C22-26) did not increase, whereas in Ormdl1/3 double KO sciatic nerve, dihydroceramides with very long chain fatty acids were highly elevated.
evidence: This claim is supported by sphingolipid measurements in brain and sciatic nerve shown in the figures.

claim: Differences exist between brain and sciatic nerve tissues, either in the flux of sphingolipid substrate through the pathway or in regulation by ORMDLs.
source: This result suggests that differences exist between these tissues, either in the flux of sphingolipid substrate through the pathway or in regulation by ORMDLs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential effects on very long chain dihydroceramides in brain versus sciatic nerve.

claim: Tight regulatory control of sphingolipid synthesis via the ORMDLs is necessary to prevent nervous system damage during myelination.
source: We have now shown that tight regulatory control of sphingolipid synthesis via the ORMDLs is also necessary to prevent nervous system damage during myelination, which relies on a large pool of mature sphingolipids.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing nervous system damage in Ormdl1/3 double KO mice.

claim: Genetic blocks in the sphingolipid metabolic pathway, especially in lysosomal degradation, cause severe neurodegeneration.
source: It is well known that genetic blocks in the sphingolipid metabolic pathway, especially in lysosomal degradation, cause severe neurodegeneration (Dunn et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.
